0.0.n: A standard daytime greeting, with final は pronounced わ.

0.2.n: This is the first piece of the nickname さゆりんご, not a separate word here.

0.3.n: This is the middle piece of the nickname さゆりんご, not a separate word here.

0.4.n: Although りんご means apple alone, here it completes the nickname さゆりんご.

0.5.n: Politely ends her self-introduction; the subject I is left unspoken.

1.0.n: An upbeat signal that she is moving on to the main activity.

1.2.n: Together with わけで, this introduces the next topic or situation.

1.3.n: Literally refers to a reason or circumstance, but というわけで works as a conversational transition here.

1.4.n: Connects わけ to what follows, completing the transition というわけで.

1.6.n: Names the time being introduced as the topic.

1.7.n: Marks 今日 as the topic: she is explaining what she is doing today.

1.8.n: In 今日はですね, this adds politeness while she pauses before continuing.

1.9.n: Softens the pause and draws the listener into what she is about to say.

1.11.n: Points out the restaurant where she is now.

1.13.n: This begins the restaurant name くるまや; it does not refer to a separate car here.

1.14.n: Completes くるまや, part of the restaurant name; や commonly appears in shop names.

1.15.n: This is the final part of the restaurant name くるまやラーメン.

1.17.n: Added to the restaurant name to sound friendly and respectful, even though it is not a person.

1.18.n: Marks the restaurant as the destination of her arrival.

1.19.n: やってくる becomes やってまいる in humble speech; ました makes it polite and past.

2.0.n: A drawn-out exclamation expressing delighted excitement.

2.2.n: This adjective can stand alone as an exclamation; I am is understood.

3.0.n: Starts というわけで, a familiar phrase for moving the conversation forward.

3.1.n: Part of というわけで, which connects her next comment to the situation already introduced.

3.2.n: Completes というわけで and links it to her next statement.

3.3.n: She names herself as the subject without adding a particle, which is common in casual speech.

3.5.n: The plain form comes before の to describe the activity of coming here.

3.6.n: Turns 来る into an activity she can describe as a first-time experience.

3.7.n: Describes this visit as her first; conversational speech leaves out は after 来るの.

3.8.n: The connecting form of だ links her first-time experience to her wish to visit.

3.9.n: 来る becomes 来たい for wanting to come, then 来たかった for a past wish.

3.10.n: Gives her prior wish to visit as a reason for wanting to enjoy herself now.

3.12.n: 楽しむ changes to 楽しみたい with たい to express what she wants to do.

3.13.n: Marks 楽しみたい as the thought expressed by 思います.

3.14.n: The polite form of 思う; after たいと, it presents her intention gently.

4.0.n: Signals the transition from introducing the visit to starting the food segment.

4.2.n: Borrowed from English and used playfully before もぐもぐ.

4.3.n: A sound-symbolic expression depicting chewing, used here as a cute invitation to eat.

0.tip: さゆりんご is one nickname, despite being split into three tappable pieces.

1.lit: Alright, so, today, you see, here, to Kurumaya Ramen, I have come!
1.tip: やってまいりました is a humble, polite way to announce that you have arrived.

2.tip: Japanese often leaves out I am when an adjective directly expresses the speaker's feelings.

3.lit: So, I, coming is a first, and because I wanted to come, I think I want to enjoy myself!
3.tip: たいと思います often expresses a gentle intention rather than uncertainty about what you want.

4.tip: もぐもぐ depicts chewing, making this a playful catchphrase rather than a standard verb phrase.
